judgments.reasoning_cat1: The legend is a plain statement of the claims-made-and-reported trigger and the defense-costs-within-limits structure; no term in it carries two reasonable meanings, and the phrase "pursuant to the terms herein" defers to the operative text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It tracks Insuring Agreement I and Section V.A (defense costs eroding the limit), so it is consistent with the whole; the only slight friction is that it makes no mention of the Awareness Provision's deeming mechanism in Section VI.A.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The item is a filled-in declaration ("125 percent of annualized premium", "One Year") whose content is definite, though the heading is rendered "Item $6" and the OCR garbling of item numbers could be argued as a mechanical slip.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches Section II.C, which grants a one-year Extended Reporting Period at the premium "required by the Insurer in Item 5(A)", so the cross-reference works; nothing else in the policy contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence conditions validity on countersignature by "another duly authorized representative of the Insurer", which is definite, although one could quibble whether the pre-printed officer signatures satisfy it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the policy addresses execution formalities, and Section VIII.K's requirement that endorsements be signed by an authorized representative is consistent with it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard consideration-and-reliance recital; "all information provided to the Insurer" is broad but its operative effect is supplied elsewhere rather than here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels Section VIII.B, which makes application statements the basis of the policy, and Section VIII.K's entire-agreement sentence; the reliance language and the entire-agreement clause coexist without a real clash.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant contains two reporting standards in one breath — "as soon as practicable after any Insured first becomes aware" plus a hard sixty-day outside limit — and "as soon as practicable" is the kind of elastic phrase parties litigate over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section VI.A (a Potential Claim noticed in the Policy Period converts a later Claim into one made in that period) and Section VI.C (notice within sixty days after the Claim is made), the outer sixty-days-after-expiry cap is hard to reconcile for claims arising long after expiry.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The spousal extension is carefully bounded by the "solely by reason of" conditions and expressly excludes claims alleging the spouse's own wrongdoing, leaving little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It dovetails with the definitions of Insured Individual and Loss, and no other provision purports to cover or exclude spouses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The extension identifies its beneficiaries by an enumerated list (estates, heirs, legal representatives, assigns) and carves out their own wrongful acts; the wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with Section VIII.I (bankruptcy) and the Insured Individual definition, with no competing provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The trigger — Insurer non-renewal or Parent Company cancellation — is stated definitely, but the clause both grants the right to "the Policyholder or the Insured Individuals" and requires election "by the Insured", and the run-together "Insuredand" is a mechanical blemish.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Item 5, Section V.A and Section VIII.C: the ERP right omits the case of Insurer cancellation for nonpayment, which the next sentence then addresses, so the pieces harmonise, though Section VIII.J's carve-out for ERP notice adds a wrinkle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any other such documents submitted in connection with the underwriting" is an open-ended catch-all appended to enumerated items, and the sweep-in of "any publicly available documents" filed with the DOL or EEOC leaves the boundary of the Application genuinely uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds Section VIII.B, which makes all such statements "the basis of this Policy", so an expansive reading of Application enlarges the misrepresentation defence; that interaction is arguable but not internally contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any other payment to or for the benefit of an employee arising out of the employment relationship" is a broad residual clause following specific examples, and the carve-out for salary and wages does not fully resolve its reach.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matters for Loss exclusions 4 and 6 and Exclusion IV.B.1; those provisions use Benefits consistently, so no conflict was found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line definition, but "implied employment contract" is inherently open-textured and could be argued to reach at-will relationships or handbook-based obligations.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with Exclusion IV.A.4 and IV.B.3, which limit recovery of amounts owed under express contracts; those carve-backs are coherent with this broad definition.
judgments.clause_name: III.C. Definition — Breach of Employment Contract

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "A written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief" is the classic battleground for what counts as a Claim, and subparagraph c. has lost its letter label in the text, compounding scope uncertainty against the enumerated proceedings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with the Potential Claim definition, Section VI.A's deeming rule and Section V.A's "deemed one Claim" language, the point at which a Claim is first made under this definition is where the instrument's timing machinery either fits or does not.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses" is a standard but genuinely evaluative limit, and the parenthetical carve-out of insureds' own wages/overhead is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used consistently in Section V.A (defense costs erode the limit), Section V.C (consent) and Exclusion IV.B (defense-costs-only), with no contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is tied to violation of statute, regulation, ordinance or common law "concerning discrimination in employment", a definite anchor rather than a vague standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Exclusion IV.A.5's list of excluded statutes (including the FLSA and ERISA) without contradiction; the Equal Pay Act carve-back is deliberate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list is mechanically defective — the fifth item has lost its number and item 1 reads "duly appointed officer" in the singular — and "solely" qualifies items 3 and 5 in ways that are hard to apply.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Compared with the Insured Individual definition, which requires a written indemnity agreement for leased persons and contractors, and with Third Party Claim, which excludes contractors' claims, the two membership lists diverge in ways a party could exploit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Item 3, "illegal work related harassment", is a general catch-all following two specifically sexual categories, raising an ejusdem generis question about whether non-sexual harassment is covered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Harassment is used in the Wrongful Employment Act definition and as a predicate for Other Workplace Tort; those uses are consistent with either reading, so no internal conflict appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A two-element definition with no evaluative language; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Insured Individual and Policyholder definitions used throughout the insuring and exclusion clauses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list is enumerated and each qualification (written indemnity agreement, direction of labour) is stated definitely, though "functional equivalent" in item 1 is somewhat elastic.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its overlap and mismatch with the Employee definition (contractors and leased persons treated differently) is the point to watch, since Insuring Agreement A turns on a Claim by or on behalf of an Employee.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction, cause or series of causally or logically connected" facts is famously indeterminate — "logically connected" has no stable boundary and is regularly litigated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It drives Section V.A's single-claim deeming rule and Exclusion IV.A.2(b)'s prior-claim sweep, so its breadth determines whether otherwise covered claims are pushed into an earlier policy year.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is long but largely enumerated; the residual pieces — "matters uninsurable under the law applicable to this Policy" and the severance/notice-period carve-out in item 6 — are the vague edges.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Loss exclusions 4 and 6 (future salary, severance) sit against Exclusion IV.B.1's carve-back for wrongful termination claims, creating a real question whether such amounts are wholly excluded or merely defense-costs-only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list is mechanically corrupted (two items numbered 4, a jump to 8, "detention imprisonment" missing a conjunction), and "failure to grant or adopt adequate employment related policies" turns on the vague word "adequate".
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The tail limiting these torts to claims alleging Breach of Employment Contract, Discrimination, Harassment, Retaliation or Wrongful Job Action fits the Wrongful Employment Act definition, so the fit is coherent even if the list is untidy.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure pointer to Item 1 of the Declarations, which names FINRA; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used consistently in the Policyholder, Subsidiary, notice and cancellation provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is definite, keyed to the Parent Company and Subsidiaries with an express debtor-in-possession inclusion.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It aligns with the Subsidiary definition and Section VIII.A.2's statement that receivership or debtor-in-possession status is not an acquisition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The substance is a plain cross-reference, but the reference is garbled as "Section VLC" when the cancellation provision is VIII.C — a mechanical citation error.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section VIII.C.3 ("The Policy Period shall end at that time"), the intended target is clear and the provisions cohere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any substance ... exhibiting any hazardous characteristics" plus an open-ended "shall also mean any other air emission, odor ... noise" list is very broad, so the outer boundary of Pollutants is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used only in Exclusion IV.A.7, whose retaliation carve-back is coherent with this definition; no other provision pulls against it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "An allegation or accusation, by or on behalf of a potential claimant" that "subsequently may give rise to a Claim" is inherently indeterminate — how formal or specific the accusation must be is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the hinge of Section VI.A's deeming mechanism and its boundary with the Claim definition in III.D determines which policy year responds, a genuine point of internal tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is closed and specific, naming ADEA, EPA and FMLA liquidated damages; little room for argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Loss exclusion 9 and the Item 6 punitive-damages election, though the garbled Declarations checkbox for Item 6 is the only soft spot.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Illegal retaliatory treatment of Employees" followed by an inclusive list is broad but tethered to illegality, so the definition is workable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly carved back out of Exclusions IV.A.5 and IV.A.7, and those carve-backs are consistent with this definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ownership and voting tests are numeric and definite; the flaw is the corrupted internal cross-reference ("Section VHLA.1").
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The referenced Section VIII.A.1 sets a 10% employee-count condition for automatic Subsidiary status, so the two must be read together and the reference, once corrected, coheres.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Is, or attempted to be, a customer or vendor" is an unusual and imprecise formulation, and the exclusion of independent contractors' claims sits oddly beside a definition otherwise framed by customer/vendor status.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Third Party Claim coverage depends on the Item 7 election, which in this Declarations page is rendered with both boxes marked, and the contractor exclusion pulls against the Employee definition's inclusion of contractors.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure aggregating definition of two other defined terms; nothing evaluative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used consistently in the insuring clause, exclusions and Section VIII.A; no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Item 3, "any other persons for whom the Insureds are legally responsible", is a general catch-all following specific categories, and its reach beyond the enumerated insureds is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits properly on top of the Breach of Employment Contract, Discrimination, Harassment, Retaliation, Wrongful Job Action and Other Workplace Tort definitions; no contradiction found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Item 4's "adverse change in the terms, conditions or status of employment" and item 3's "deprivation of a career opportunity" are open-textured phrases whose boundaries are contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds the Wrongful Employment Act definition and the Exclusion IV.B.1 carve-back for wrongful termination, both of which use it coherently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition opens with a very wide list of conduct ("any error, misstatement ... breach of duty") and closes with "on any other basis prohibited by law", a residual after a long enumeration of protected characteristics.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the Third Party Claim definition and Insuring Agreement B's Item 7 condition; no operative provision pulls the other way.
judgments.clause_name: III.Z. Definition — Wrongful Third Party Act

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Repeated "in any way involving" prefaces and the sweep-in of "any other federal, state local or foreign statute or law similar to any statute or law described in (a) through (h)" put a broad catch-all against a detailed enumeration, the classic ejusdem generis problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusions A.1 and A.2, read with the Interrelated Wrongful Acts definition and Section V.A's deeming rule, can push a reported claim into a prior policy year, and the Retaliation carve-backs must be squared with the Retaliation definition.
judgments.clause_name: IV.A. Exclusions Applicable to All Loss

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The structure is clear (defense costs only), but B.4's "any other equitable remedy" following injunctive, declaratory and restitutionary relief is a catch-all of uncertain reach, and B.1's wrongful-termination carve-back is undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be reconciled with Loss exclusions 4 and 6, which exclude future salary and severance from Loss altogether; whether those amounts are excluded or merely defense-costs-only is a genuine internal question.
judgments.clause_name: IV.B. Exclusions Applicable Solely To Loss other than Defense Costs

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The wording is largely numeric and definite, but the deeming sentence — a Claim is first made on the earlier of first assertion or notice "under this Policy or any prior policy" — imports facts outside this instrument and turns on the vague Interrelated Wrongful Acts concept.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its final sentence limits coverage to Claims "deemed" first made in the Policy Period, which must be reconciled with Section II.C's ERP deeming and Section VI.A's Potential Claim deeming; the three mechanisms overlap.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence tying liability to Loss in excess of a stated dollar Retention; entirely definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Item 4 and with Section V.C's fifty-percent-of-retention consent threshold.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three evaluative standards appear — consent "not be unreasonably withheld", insureds who "unreasonably refuse to consent", and cooperation the Insurer "reasonably requests" — each a familiar site of dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The duty to defend here sits against Exclusion IV.B's defense-costs-only regime and Section V.A's erosion of the limit, and those provisions are expressly harmonised in the text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is mechanically clear, but its operation depends entirely on the elastic Potential Claim definition, and the last sentence's cut-off for "fees and expenses incurred prior to the time such circumstances result in a Claim" invites argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It deems a later Claim made in an earlier Policy Period, which must be squared with Insuring Agreement I's requirement that the Claim be first made in the Policy Period and reported within sixty days of its expiry.
judgments.clause_name: VI.A. Awareness Provision — Notice of Potential Claim

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The required contents are enumerated, but the catch-all in subparagraph 2 ("such additional information and cooperation as it may reasonably require") and its framing as a condition precedent make the compliance threshold arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports Section VI.A and Section VIII.H's full-compliance condition; consistent with the whole.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "As soon as practicable" with a hard sixty-day backstop is a familiar formula; the sixty-day period runs from a definite event (when the Claim is first made).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits notice long after the Policy Period ends, which is hard to square with Insuring Agreement I's absolute bar on reporting later than sixty days after expiry of the Policy Period.
judgments.clause_name: VI.C. Awareness Provision — Notice of Subsequent Claim

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The deeming sentence — notices effective on actual receipt "or one day following the date such notices are sent, whichever is earlier" — is internally odd, since sending plus one day may precede receipt, and the address reference is mistyped as "Item 711".
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Item 11's separate claim and general notice addresses and with Section VIII.J's authorization clause; no substantive conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The two employee-count tests (automatic Subsidiary status only if the acquired entity is under 10%, ninety-day cover only if the post-Transaction headcount exceeds 110%) leave the middle band unaddressed, and "as for a period of ninety (90) days" is grammatically broken.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Subsidiary definition expressly incorporates this subsection, so the gap in its conditions leaves the status of mid-sized acquisitions unresolved across the instrument.
judgments.clause_name: VIII.A.1. Transactions That Impact Coverage — Acquisitions

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The triggering events are stated in definite percentage and asset terms, and the run-off effect (cover only for pre-event Wrongful Acts) is spelled out.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its statement that coverage "shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company" collides on its face with Section VIII.C.1, which lets the Parent Company cancel during the Policy Period.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short run-off rule with a definite temporal cut-off; the only slip is "until termination of the Policy" rather than the Policy Period.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels Section VIII.A.2's run-off language and the Subsidiary definition's "so long as" wording, and no provision contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reliance and incorporation language is standard, but it never states the consequence (rescission? avoidance of the claim?) of an inaccurate statement, and the severability paragraphs are garbled in numbering.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its breadth turns on the very wide Application definition in III.A, and the entire-agreement sentence in Section VIII.K sits alongside the incorporation of application statements; the two are reconcilable but arguable.
judgments.clause_name: VIII.B. Representations and Severability with Respect to Application

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Each subparagraph gives a definite notice period and mechanism, and subparagraph 6 defers to longer statutory periods; little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with Section VIII.A.2 (non-cancellable after a change of control) and Section II.C (ERP available on Parent cancellation or Insurer non-renewal), and the first of those creates a limit on the cancellation right stated here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The excess clause is confined by its terms to "Loss arising from any Third Party Claim", and the following sentence says the policy is "intended to provide primary insurance" in all other events — "intended to" is softer than an operative statement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else addresses other insurance, and the Third Party Claim limitation matches the Item 7 election structure; no conflict found beyond the garbled Item 7 checkbox.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence of worldwide territorial scope, with no qualifying language to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the worldwide references in the Discrimination and Pollutants definitions and in Exclusion IV.A.5; consistent throughout.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The conversion mechanism names a specific source and a specific date, leaving no evaluative judgment.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the dollar-denominated Limits and Retention in Items 3 and 4; no competing provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard subrogation to the extent of payment plus a cooperation covenant; the terms are definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with Section VIII.H and the cooperation duty in Section V.C without tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Full compliance with all the terms of this Policy" as a condition precedent is broad and its strictness (material versus literal compliance) is the kind of point parties argue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reinforces the condition-precedent language in Section VI.B and the notice provisions; no contradiction with any operative term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, symmetrical statement preserving obligations and defences; nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Policyholder definition's debtor-in-possession inclusion and Section II.B's extension to representatives of insolvent individuals.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The agency grant is enumerated (notices, premiums, endorsements) with an express carve-out for ERP election notice; the wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-out must be read with Section II.C, which allows the Policyholder or the Insured Individuals to elect the ERP, and the two fit together rather than clashing.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The endorsement requirement and non-waiver sentence are definite, though the non-waiver sentence's reference to knowledge of "the Insurer, the Insureds or any agent" is loosely drafted.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The entire-agreement statement sits against Section VIII.B, which incorporates Application statements as "part of this Policy"; that is reconcilable but is the one point of friction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional headings clause with no operative content and nothing evaluative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the policy's heavy use of Item and Section cross-references, which reference numbers rather than captions.
